conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you could come in today. My name is Maya Bennett, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers. To help me understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, I’d like to use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply ten questions about the past week, and it helps us see if you might benefit from a little extra support or resources. Everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise, and there’s no right or wrong answer—just whatever feels true for you. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the questions conversationally; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it one step at a time. Does that sound okay?

Let’s begin. Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

(soft sigh) Honestly, I haven’t really felt like laughing. My sister sent me a funny video yesterday and I just… stared at it. I used to laugh at everything, but lately even when something is sort of amusing, the smile fades right away.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

(looking down at my lap)  
Not really… I mean, I can force a little chuckle if someone’s watching, but nothing feels truly funny inside. It’s like the laughter gets stuck.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

(shakes head slowly)  
No… not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels flat. I make plans because I “should,” but inside I’m just… empty about them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

(eyes water a little)  
Yeah… a lot, actually. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I missed some cue or I’m not soothing her right. Yesterday she wouldn’t nap and I kept replaying everything I did—like, maybe I didn’t swaddle tight enough or I drank too much caffeine. My head knows babies just cry, but my heart keeps whispering it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

(nods, twisting the edge of my sleeve)  
Pretty much all the time. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly picture her choking, or I’ll check if she’s breathing every twenty minutes at night. There’s no real reason—she’s healthy, the pediatrician says so—but I can’t stop the “what-ifs” from looping.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

(hands clasped tight in my lap)  
Yes… sometimes my heart just starts racing out of nowhere. I’ll be folding her onesies and suddenly feel like I can’t catch my breath, like something awful is about to happen. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary, and there’s no real trigger—I know rationally I’m safe, but my body doesn’t listen.
Things have been getting on top of me

(nods slowly, voice low)  
Yes… most days feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, she wants to nurse again, the dog’s whining, and I just stand there frozen, thinking, “I can’t do all this.” I still get through it—she’s fed, changed, loved—but it feels like I’m sprinting on empty and the tiniest extra thing could tip me over.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

(quietly)  
Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps spinning—did I sterilize the bottles right, is she too hot, am I cut out for this? Some nights I fall asleep okay, then jolt awake at 2 a.m. and can’t drift off again. It’s like the sadness just buzzes under my skin and won’t let me rest.
I have felt sad or miserable

(swallows hard, eyes on the floor)  
Most of the time. It’s like there’s this gray cloud parked over me—I can still do what I have to, but everything feels heavy and colorless. I’ll watch her smile and think, “This should make me happy,” yet the sadness just sits there anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah... a few times this week. Once it was just because I dropped a plate and it shattered—totally normal thing—but I sat on the kitchen floor and cried. Other times it’s quieter, like tears slipping out while I rock her at 3 a.m. It feels like the sadness needs somewhere to go, so it turns into tears whether I want it to or not.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

(shakes head quickly, eyes wide)  
No—never. I feel low, but I would never want to leave her or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant undisclosed age)  
Date: [today]  
Screener: [licensed MHP]

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS items paraphrased):  
- Marked anhedonia (loss of laughter, enjoyment)  
- Pervasive low mood, “colorless,” frequent crying spells  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt re infant care  
- Persistent, intrusive “what-if” worries; nocturnal safety-checking  
- Episodic panic symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness)  
- Subjective overwhelm / “drowning” in daily tasks  
- Initial & middle insomnia linked to rumination  
- NO self-harm ideation (endorsed item 10 negatively)

Pattern: Symptoms present most days for at least the past week; cause functional difficulty but patient continues to meet infant’s basic needs.

Screening significance  
- Total EPDS items suggest elevated risk for major postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety  
- Absence of self-harm ideation lowers acute safety risk; nevertheless, severity of mood/anxiety symptoms warrants prompt referral for comprehensive evaluation and possible treatment.

Risk factors documented: anhedonia, guilt, sleep disruption, panic spells, feeling overwhelmed.

Next step: Recommend expedited referral to OB mental-health team or perinatal psychiatrist for formal assessment and care planning.
